name: torlink
description: 👾 A sleek, zero-setup torrent finder and downloader that lives right in your terminal.
readmeExcerpt:
Finding a torrent these days sucks. One site is a minefield of fake download buttons. Another hides the real link under a popup that spawns two more tabs. And after all that, half the results are dead, zero seeders. torlink is a torrent finder that lives in your terminal, with zero setup and nothing to configure. One search checks a short, curated list of reputable sources at once, and whatever you pick downloads straight to your computer. The files are yours, saved to your downloads folder. ## Get started 1. **Install Node** (from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org)), it's all torlink needs. 2. **Open your terminal.** 3. **Start it:** ```sh npx torlnk ``` That's the only thing you'll type. torlink opens straight to a search bar: search for what you want, paste in a magnet link or a bare infohash, drag a `.torrent` file from your file manager onto the window, or just press Enter on an empty box to browse the curated library. From there it's all keypresses, nothing to memorize, and `?` brings up the full list anytime. ## Finding something Type what you're looking for and press Enter. Results stream in from every source as they answer, tagged with size and how many people are sharing each one, so you can see what'll come down fast. Arrow to a result and press `d` to save it, or press space on several rows and then `d` to download them together. `shift+d` picks a folder for the current result or marked batch.

## Your downloads Active downloads sit up top with their progress, speed, and time left; when one finishes it drops into Recently downloaded just below, so the list stays tidy. Everything's still there when you come back, and anything interrupted picks up where it left off. Downloads run in the background while you keep searching, so you can queue up as many as you want. They save to your downloads folder, and the Downloads pane keeps tabs on each one; press `o` anytime to change where that is, or use `shift+d` to send a result or marked batch somewhere else without changing the default. When something finishes it keeps seeding automatically so the next person can find it too, and the Seeding tab lets you pause or stop that anytime.

When a download comes with several videos or tracks, torlink drops a `playlist.m3u` into each folder holding more than one, so a course split into modules plays straight through in order. Run `torlnk --no-playlist` if you'd rather it didn't. ## What it searches A short, hand-picked list of trusted sources: | Category | Sources | | --- | --- | | Games | FitGirl | | Movies | YTS, The Pirate Bay, BitTorrented | | TV | EZTV, The Pirate Bay, BitTorrented | | Anime | Nyaa, SubsPlease | Games are the only category that can run code, so they come from FitGirl alone, a repacker with a long, trusted track record; everything else is plain video and subtitles. If a source is down, the search carries on without it, and torlink tells you which one is offline. ## Headless torlink also runs without the TUI, for servers and seedboxes: torlnk search "" [--category games|movies|tv|anime] print one JSON document of merged search results torlnk seed share files you already have torlnk watch download anything dropped into a folder torlnk serve take magnets over HTTP torlnk files stream finished downloads over HTTP torlnk attach keep the TUI alive across ssh sessions Add `--daemon` to keep seed, watch, serve, or files running after you log out; `torlnk --help` has the full list of modes and flags. ### Sharing something of your own Everything else starts with a torrent someone else made. `seed` goes the other way: torlnk seed ./album It turns the folder into a torrent, saves `album.torrent` next to it, prints the magnet, and starts sharing right away. Send anyone the magnet and they pull the files from you. ### Driving it over HTTP `serve` takes a magnet or a `.torrent` you already have: POST /add {"magnet":"magnet:?xt=..."} POST /add {"torrent":""} Either can carry a `seedTime` for that one torrent, in the same grammar as `--seed-time` (`"30d"`, `"2h"`; `0` means never stop). It wins over the daemon-wide flag, so a box that normally drops seeds after a couple of hours can keep one release alive for a month. Change it later, or on something already downloading, through the control endpoint; `GET /downloads` reports the limit and when it falls due (`seedUntil`): POST /control {"id":"","action":"seed-time","seedTime":"30d"} ### Binding to a VPN or interface If torrents should only ever leave through one interface, name it: torlnk serve --interface wg0 --peer-port 51413 Every peer, tracker, DHT and search socket is bound to that interface's IPv4 address, and the fixed peer port is the one to forward. If the interface drops, downloads and seeds pause instead of taking another route, and pick up on their own when it is back. The same flags work on `watch`, `seed` and the TUI, or as `TORLINK_INTERFACE`, `TORLINK_PEER_PORT` and `TORLINK_DHT_PORT`, with nothing new on screen. `serve` reports the state on `GET /network` and takes changes on `POST /network` without a restart. torlink knows nothing about any particular VPN, only the interface; `torlnk --help` has the details and limits. ## Contributing To run or work on torlink locally: 1. Clone the repository and open the folder. 2. Install dependencies: ```sh npm install ``` 3. Run the development version: ```sh npm run dev ``` Or build it and run the bundled version: ```sh npm run build npx torlnk ``` Before opening a PR, skim [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md); it lays out the bar with examples from real merged PRs. ## Privacy Your files stay on your disk, and nothing routes through a central server; torlink only talks to the torrent network directly. Once a download finishes it keeps seeding by default, sharing it back so the next person can find it just as easily. The network only works because people pass things along, and even a few minutes makes a real difference. If you'd rather not, opt out anytime: open the Seeding tab, press `p` to pause or stop any item, and press it again to pick it back up. Always your call.
readmeHtml:
Finding a torrent these days sucks. One site is a minefield of fake download buttons. Another hides the real link under a popup that spawns two more tabs. And after all that, half the results are dead, zero seeders.

torlink is a torrent finder that lives in your terminal, with zero setup and nothing to configure. One search checks a short, curated list of reputable sources at once, and whatever you pick downloads straight to your computer. The files are yours, saved to your downloads folder.

Get started

  1. Install Node (from nodejs.org), it's all torlink needs.

  2. Open your terminal.

  3. Start it:

    npx torlnk

That's the only thing you'll type. torlink opens straight to a search bar: search for what you want, paste in a magnet link or a bare infohash, drag a .torrent file from your file manager onto the window, or just press Enter on an empty box to browse the curated library. From there it's all keypresses, nothing to memorize, and ? brings up the full list anytime.

Finding something

Type what you're looking for and press Enter. Results stream in from every source as they answer, tagged with size and how many people are sharing each one, so you can see what'll come down fast. Arrow to a result and press d to save it, or press space on several rows and then d to download them together. shift+d picks a folder for the current result or marked batch.

Your downloads

Active downloads sit up top with their progress, speed, and time left; when one finishes it drops into Recently downloaded just below, so the list stays tidy. Everything's still there when you come back, and anything interrupted picks up where it left off.

Downloads run in the background while you keep searching, so you can queue up as many as you want. They save to your downloads folder, and the Downloads pane keeps tabs on each one; press o anytime to change where that is, or use shift+d to send a result or marked batch somewhere else without changing the default. When something finishes it keeps seeding automatically so the next person can find it too, and the Seeding tab lets you pause or stop that anytime.

When a download comes with several videos or tracks, torlink drops a playlist.m3u into each folder holding more than one, so a course split into modules plays straight through in order. Run torlnk --no-playlist if you'd rather it didn't.

What it searches

A short, hand-picked list of trusted sources:

Category Sources
Games FitGirl
Movies YTS, The Pirate Bay, BitTorrented
TV EZTV, The Pirate Bay, BitTorrented
Anime Nyaa, SubsPlease

Games are the only category that can run code, so they come from FitGirl alone, a repacker with a long, trusted track record; everything else is plain video and subtitles. If a source is down, the search carries on without it, and torlink tells you which one is offline.

Headless

torlink also runs without the TUI, for servers and seedboxes:

torlnk search "<query>" [--category games|movies|tv|anime]
                        print one JSON document of merged search results
torlnk seed <path>    share files you already have
torlnk watch <dir>    download anything dropped into a folder
torlnk serve          take magnets over HTTP
torlnk files          stream finished downloads over HTTP
torlnk attach         keep the TUI alive across ssh sessions

Add --daemon to keep seed, watch, serve, or files running after you log out; torlnk --help has the full list of modes and flags.

Sharing something of your own

Everything else starts with a torrent someone else made. seed goes the other way:

torlnk seed ./album

It turns the folder into a torrent, saves album.torrent next to it, prints the magnet, and starts sharing right away. Send anyone the magnet and they pull the files from you.

Driving it over HTTP

serve takes a magnet or a .torrent you already have:

POST /add {"magnet":"magnet:?xt=..."}
POST /add {"torrent":"<base64>"}

Either can carry a seedTime for that one torrent, in the same grammar as --seed-time ("30d", "2h"; 0 means never stop). It wins over the daemon-wide flag, so a box that normally drops seeds after a couple of hours can keep one release alive for a month. Change it later, or on something already downloading, through the control endpoint; GET /downloads reports the limit and when it falls due (seedUntil):

POST /control {"id":"<info hash>","action":"seed-time","seedTime":"30d"}

Binding to a VPN or interface

If torrents should only ever leave through one interface, name it:

torlnk serve --interface wg0 --peer-port 51413

Every peer, tracker, DHT and search socket is bound to that interface's IPv4 address, and the fixed peer port is the one to forward. If the interface drops, downloads and seeds pause instead of taking another route, and pick up on their own when it is back. The same flags work on watch, seed and the TUI, or as TORLINK_INTERFACE, TORLINK_PEER_PORT and TORLINK_DHT_PORT, with nothing new on screen. serve reports the state on GET /network and takes changes on POST /network without a restart. torlink knows nothing about any particular VPN, only the interface; torlnk --help has the details and limits.

Contributing

To run or work on torlink locally:

  1. Clone the repository and open the folder.
  2. Install dependencies: 
    npm install
  3. Run the development version: 
    npm run dev
    Or build it and run the bundled version: 
    npm run build
npx torlnk

Before opening a PR, skim CONTRIBUTING.md; it lays out the bar with examples from real merged PRs.

Privacy

Your files stay on your disk, and nothing routes through a central server; torlink only talks to the torrent network directly. Once a download finishes it keeps seeding by default, sharing it back so the next person can find it just as easily. The network only works because people pass things along, and even a few minutes makes a real difference. If you'd rather not, opt out anytime: open the Seeding tab, press p to pause or stop any item, and press it again to pick it back up. Always your call.

releases.name: v1.11.1
releases.body:
> Opening a magnet or .torrent while torlink is already running now adds it to that window instead of starting a second one.

**One window.** Run `torlnk` with a magnet or a `.torrent` while the TUI is open, and it is added to that window. The second launch hands it over and exits.

**Several at once.** Files opened together all land in the same window, including ones that arrive while it is still starting up.

**Recovers after a crash.** A socket file left behind by a crashed session is replaced by the next launch.

**Clearer prompts.** The `m` key now reads "Paste magnet or .torrent", and `--help` says where a launch goes.

**Lighter searches.** A search that retries failing sources no longer leaves their unfinished responses holding sockets and memory.

```
npx torlnk
```

releases.name: v1.11.0
releases.body:
> torlink can now keep your torrents on your VPN: name the interface, and if the tunnel drops, downloads and seeds pause instead of falling back to your real connection.

**Bind to a VPN or any interface.** Start torlink with `--interface wg0` (or `tun0`, `NordLynx`, or the address itself) and every peer, tracker, DHT and search connection goes out from that interface. It works in the TUI, `serve`, `watch` and `seed`, or through `TORLINK_INTERFACE`.

**Pauses when the tunnel drops.** If the interface goes away, downloads and seeds stop rather than take another route, and pick up on their own when it is back, on its new address if that changed.

**Fixed ports.** `--peer-port` pins the listen port so one forward on the VPN side covers it, and `--dht-port` pins the DHT.

**Network over HTTP.** `serve` reports the binding on `GET /network`, including how many peers dialed in, and `POST /network` changes the interface or ports without a restart, so a script can hand over a forwarded port when the VPN moves it.

**Lighter long runs.** A daemon left running for days no longer piles up UDP sockets and memory, since outgoing uTP peers now share one socket.

releases.name: v1.10.0
releases.body:
> This release lets you grab a whole batch at once: mark results with space, then download them together.

**Also on git.bairon.dev.** torlink's code is now also hosted at [git.bairon.dev/baairon/torlink](https://git.bairon.dev/baairon/torlink). Issues and pull requests stay here on GitHub, and nothing changes for installs.

**Batch downloads.** Press space to mark or unmark the result under the cursor, then press `d` to download every marked torrent, or `D` to pick one folder for all of them. With nothing marked, `d` and `D` work on the highlighted row as before.

**Marks hold steady.** Marks survive re-sorting and newly streamed results, and clear on a new search or category. Rows hidden by the filter are skipped, so nothing downloads unseen.

**Batch-aware folder prompt.** The `D` prompt shows how many torrents are marked and their total size, and cancelling it keeps the marks.

```
npx torlnk
```

releases.name: v1.9.1
releases.body:
> A stuck source no longer stalls a search, and a big seed keeps seeding through a restart.

- **Headless search has a deadline**: `torlnk search` takes `--timeout` (default `45s`, same grammar as `--seed-time`). When time runs out, sources that already answered still print, and any source that didn't is reported with code `"timeout"`. A source asking to retry later than the 20s backoff cap now fails right away with its HTTP status instead of holding up the whole search. (#196)
- **Large seeds survive a restart**: a restored seed's grace period now starts after torlink finishes checking the pieces already on disk, so a big torrent with a few pieces to repair keeps seeding instead of being stopped and marked missing.
- **FitGirl search finds the exact title**: results now sort by relevance instead of date, so a title made of common words no longer gets buried under newer posts that merely mention them. (#198), thanks to @danielshefer1

```
npx torlnk
```

releases.name: v1.9.0
releases.body:
> Multi-file downloads finish with a playlist, and one torrent can now carry its own seed limit.

- **Playlists for anything with more than one track**: a finished download drops a `playlist.m3u` into every folder holding two or more audio or video files, nested folders included, ordered the way the filenames read. An existing playlist is never overwritten. Pass `--no-playlist` or set `TORLINK_NO_PLAYLIST=1` to skip it. (#192), thanks to @ralyodio
- **Give one torrent its own seed limit**: `POST /add` now takes a `seedTime` in the same grammar as `--seed-time` (`"30d"`, `"2h"`, `0` to never stop), and it wins over the daemon-wide flag. The `seed-time` control action changes it later, even mid-download, and `GET /downloads` reports the limit and when it falls due. (#186), thanks to @ralyodio
- **An escape hatch for uTP socket exhaustion**: uTP stays on by default, the way every major client ships it. Where peer counts drive it into `WSAENOBUFS` or `EMFILE`, set `TORLINK_NO_UTP` and torlink runs without it.

```
npx torlnk
```

aiSummary.oneLiner: A sleek, zero-setup terminal-based torrent finder and downloader.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Torlink is a streamlined command-line BitTorrent client built for efficiency and speed. It provides users with a way to find, download, and seed torrent files directly from a terminal interface without heavy graphical dependencies. The client focuses on low resource consumption, making it ideal for running on headless servers or single-board computers like the Raspberry Pi. It handles standard magnet links and torrent files while offering detailed terminal output regarding peer connections and transfer speeds. This allows system administrators to automate large file transfers seamlessly via scripts.
keyFeatures: Terminal interface: Provides a clean, text-based UI for managing downloads without needing a desktop environment.
Low resource footprint: Operates with minimal CPU and memory overhead compared to graphical torrent clients.
Magnet link support: Processes standard magnet URIs directly from the command line for quick download initiation.
Headless execution: Runs efficiently in the background on remote servers or NAS devices.
Detailed metrics display: Shows real-time connection speeds, peer counts, and download progress directly in the console.

useCases.title: Downloading files on servers
useCases.description: Fetch large datasets or ISO files directly onto remote headless servers.

useCases.title: Automating media retrieval
useCases.description: Integrate torrent downloading into automated bash scripts or cron jobs.

useCases.title: Running on constrained hardware
useCases.description: Manage peer-to-peer file sharing efficiently on older laptops or Raspberry Pis.

useCases.title: Managing headless seedboxes
useCases.description: Operate a low-overhead seedbox entirely through an SSH connection.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: System administrators, power users, and developers who prefer managing file downloads via the command line. Users operating headless servers requiring a lightweight torrent client.
